subject: RM_ModernBridge_anchors

reply.subject: RM_ModernBridge_anchors

observed.facings.png: Three facings at one scale, two identical anchors in each. South: a pale galvanised rectangular base plate at the top with four bolts. Below it is a dark blue-grey tapered steel body with gussets, then a light-steel clevis block with a black ring pin, and a long twisted cable running down to the bottom edge. North is the same assembly mirrored vertically: the cable comes in from the top, then the clevis, the body and the base plate at the bottom. East turns it 90 degrees: base plate on the left, tapered body, clevis, and a cable running right. The shading is simple linear gradients with crisp hard edges, more like a flat vector drawing than painted art. There is no red anywhere.
observed.south.png: Two copies of the south anchor. Grey-blue steel body, galvanised plate, a light clevis with a dark pin hole, and a cable hanging down. The edges are flat and hard.
observed.east.png: Two copies of the east anchor, lying horizontal. The plate is on the left and the cable runs right. Its visible height is shorter because the long axis is horizontal.
observed.north.png: Two copies of the north anchor. The cable comes in from the top and the base plate sits at the bottom. It is a vertical mirror of south.
observed.scale.png: At max zoom the two south anchors sit in a 1x1 cell beside a human, and the cables reach the bottom of the cell. The normal-play inset at 32 px per cell shows two tiny grey specks with lines: they can be recognised as small steel fittings, but no detail survives.
observed.variants_1.png: Three other anchor designs, two copies each, all painterly and detailed. The first is a heavy cast-steel clamp on a pedestal plate with a thick wire rope. The second is a slim steel clevis bracket with a wire rope. The third is a wooden block with steel strapping, a bolt and a rope. These have rich shading and a vanilla-like rendering that the R3 south/east/north design lacks.
observed.assembled_1.png: Offline composite: a light concrete or grating deck with yellow dashed lane lines and dark steel edge rails crosses a grey river between brown riverbanks. Four small east-facing anchors sit near each end of the deck, two at left and two at right, with short cables trailing. The anchors read as small dark steel fittings. The deck reads as a modern road bridge. Nothing reads as red or blue plumbing.

CAMERA.seen: A flat plate-and-bracket fitting seen from above at a slant, with no round tops to measure. The galvanised plate reads as a lit top face. It is a low part and nothing contradicts the building camera, though the depth cues are weak.

BORE.seen: No pipe or hose. The black ring on the clevis is a pin or bolt hole, not an open bore. The cables are solid twisted strands with no open ends shown.

PORTS.seen: assembled_1 is an offline composite, not an in-game capture. The cables end in empty deck with nothing to attach to, so it is impossible to judge whether the cable meets the tower or deck port at the same cell, height and plane.

LAYERS.seen: In the composite the anchors and cables draw over the deck, and nothing that should be behind draws in front.

ROTATIONS.seen: South, east and north show the same plate, body, clevis and cable in the same blue-grey and galvanised palette. North is a vertical mirror and east is a 90-degree turn. The 41% height spread comes from the horizontal east pose and is real, not a size jump.

SIGNATURE.seen: It is recognisable as a cable anchor: a bolted base plate, a tapered steel bracket, a clevis with a pin, and wire cable.

MATERIAL.seen: The dark blue-grey reads as painted structural steel, the pale speckled plate as galvanised or concrete, and the cable as twisted steel strand. It reads as highway-bridge steel, not as a coloured coat on plumbing.

FOOTPRINT.seen: In scale.png the anchors and cables stay inside the 1x1 outlined cell. Nothing overflows or floats tiny.

ALPHA.seen: Clean transparent background in every facing, with no shadow or ground patch. The code confirms real alpha.

OURS.seen: A simple bespoke shape that does not match any vanilla or known mod asset. The provenance is a recolour of our own kept art.

OWNER_NOTES.seen: The red trim is gone. The anchors and deck read as modern bridge steel and concrete, with no water or plumbing colour coding.

LEGIBLE.seen: At 32 px per cell the anchors are small grey fittings with a line of cable: still readable as hardware, but marginal.

findings.seen: The R3 anchor is rendered with flat linear gradients and hard vector edges, while the three anchor designs in variants_1 are richly painted with cast detail, highlights and wire-rope texture. Side by side they look like different artists.
findings.quote: reads as a different artist or size class than the owner-kept siblings
findings.fix: Render the anchor with the same painterly shading as the variants_1 anchors: cast-steel bevels, bolt highlights, worn edges and twisted wire-rope texture, keeping the blue-grey structural-steel palette.

findings.seen: The body is a plain gradient trapezoid, the plate is a flat rectangle with a noise fill, and the clevis is a gradient square with a ring. At max zoom it reads as a script-drawn diagram more than painterly vanilla art.
findings.quote: Painterly vanilla RimWorld: real anatomy, high resolution where the player looks, a clean dark outline that reads at standard zoom.
findings.fix: The anchor is painted with soft painterly light and shadow on the steel body and plate, so it holds up at 128–256 px per cell.

findings.seen: In the offline composite each anchor's cable ends a short way out on the deck with no tower or hanger to meet, so the cable-to-port join cannot be judged.
findings.quote: Parts meet their ports: each coupler, hose and cord meets its port at the same cell, height and plane, in every rotation of the assembled view.
findings.fix: An in-game capture shows each anchor cable running to its tower or deck port at the same cell and height.

reply.needs_call_why: PORTS is unreadable because the assembled panel is an offline composite, not an in-game capture. Also, the flat, script-drawn rendering differs clearly from the painterly anchors in variants_1. The geometry is the kept art and only the colour changed, so the style gap may be one the owner has already accepted.
proposals: For recolour-only candidates whose alpha is byte-identical to kept art, let the card say explicitly that the geometry and style were previously accepted, so reviewers judge colour alone and do not re-flag the style.
Show the four anchor kinds named in the title in facings.png. Here the facings show one kind and variants_1 shows three others with no labels.

subject: RM_ModernBridge_decks

reply.subject: RM_ModernBridge_decks

observed.facings.png: A single south tile on the labelled sheet. The middle is a pale grey mottled concrete deck in three slabs, separated by thin dark seams, with a bolt in each slab corner. A dashed yellow centre line runs from top to bottom. On the left and right edges are dark blue-grey steel stringers with paired light rivets at regular spacing. There is no red anywhere.
observed.south.png: The same tile alone at 256 px. The whole square is opaque: concrete slabs with the yellow dashed line between two blue-grey riveted steel side rails. There is no cast shadow and no scenery. It reads as a road deck seen from overhead.
observed.scale.png: The deck sits on one cell beside a vanilla human. At 211 px per cell it reads clearly as a concrete road slab with steel edge rails. In the 32 px per cell thumbnail it still reads as a grey tile with darker side edges, and the yellow line is faintly visible.
observed.variants_1.png: Five deck types side by side. (1) Fine galvanised bar grating with blue-grey riveted side rails. (2) Heavy deck: thick round vertical bars on hex-bolted crossbeams. (3) Medium grating with cross-bars. (4) Concrete slabs with corner bolts and no centre line. (5) Warm timber planks with visible grain, framed by blue-grey steel rails with bolted plates. The gaps in the gratings are transparent (shown white). Steel, concrete and wood all read as their materials, and all five share one blue-grey steel trim colour.
observed.assembled_1.png: An offline composite: a grated deck spans a grey river between brown riverbank dirt. Blue-grey riveted edge rails run continuously along the top and bottom of the span. The galvanised bars repeat seamlessly across the tile joins, and water and ground show through the gaps. It reads as a steel grating footbridge, not a pipe.

CAMERA.seen: A deck tile is a walkable floor surface, drawn flat as seen from above, like vanilla floors and bridges. It has no raised round top or box that would show a 35-degree elevation.

BORE.seen: There are no pipes or hoses. The heavy deck's round bars are drawn lengthwise with no open ends facing the camera.

PORTS.seen: There are no couplers, hoses or cords. In the assembled view the deck link-atlas joins meet cleanly, with continuous edge rails and gratings that line up.

LAYERS.seen: In the assembled view the deck draws over the water and the bank, and the edge rails draw over the grating edge.

ROTATIONS.seen: There is one south facing, as expected for a floor-like deck. The five variants share the same blue-grey steel trim colour.

SIGNATURE.seen: The concrete, grated, heavy, steel and timber decks are each recognisable, and the riveted steel stringers mark them as bridge decks.

MATERIAL.seen: The trim reads as painted structural steel with specular rivets. The concrete is mottled grey, the grating is galvanised silver, and the wood has visible grain.

FOOTPRINT.seen: The tile fills its 1x1 cell exactly, as a deck tile should. Measured visible-alpha height is 256 px.

ALPHA.seen: There is no backdrop, halo or painted shadow. The concrete tile is opaque by design, and the gratings have transparent gaps that show the water in the assembled view.

OURS.seen: This is a recolour of the mod's own kept FlowWorks bridge art. It does not match any vanilla bridge.

OWNER_NOTES.seen: The firetruck-red trim is gone. The blue-grey steel, the concrete with a yellow road line and the galvanised grating read as a modern highway or footbridge, not as water plumbing.

LEGIBLE.seen: In the 32 px per cell thumbnail it reads as a grey slab with dark steel edges.

findings.seen: The concrete texture is a fine, uniform noise with soft cloudy blotches. It is slightly flat and synthetic next to the steel, with no aggregate, wear or expansion-joint detail.
findings.quote: the colour reads as metal, rubber, ceramic
findings.fix: The concrete slabs show subtle aggregate grain, faint tyre wear along the lanes and a sealed expansion joint at each slab seam.

findings.seen: The timber deck's warm orange wood stands out tonally from the grey family of steel and concrete decks.
findings.quote: Rotations agree: same machine, same parts, same palette
findings.fix: The timber planks are a weathered, slightly greyed treated-lumber brown that sits beside the steel and concrete decks.

proposals: The machine template's CAMERA item assumes a raised building. Floor-like deck parts could use a 'flat walkable surface, top-down is correct' exception on the card so later reviewers do not flag CAM_WRONG.
PORTS and LAYERS could allow n/a for parts with no couplers or hoses, such as deck tiles.

blocking.fix: The timber planks are a weathered, slightly greyed treated-lumber brown that sits beside the steel and concrete decks.
